summary: Provides models and manageable objects for printing environments, covering both physical and logical entities within a printing device. It obsoletes RFC 1759.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3805 defines a standard list of values about a printer, so that monitoring tools from different vendors ask the same questions and read the same answers. It covers what the printer is made of, what state it is in, and what has gone wrong with it, such as an empty toner cartridge or a paper jam.

questions: how to monitor printers with snmp
how to monitor printer toner with snmp
subtitle: Common SNMP objects for reading a printer's configuration, its current state and the problems it reports.

tldr.problem: A management application needs one common way to ask any printer what it is, what state it is in, and what has gone wrong with it, whatever the maker.
tldr.mechanism: The Printer MIB models a printer as 13 types of sub-units and defines SNMP objects that describe each one, report its status, and list the alerts that are active.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3805 obsoletes RFC 1759 while staying backward compatible with it, and adds new objects, a new alert notification and a companion IANA-maintained MIB of enumerations.

today: RFC 3805 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 1759, and the finishing side of a printer is covered separately by RFC 3806. No later RFC in the index replaces or updates it.

sections.title: What the Printer MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3805 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for printers: a named set of values that a management application can read and, for some of them, write using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The objects apply to physical parts of a printing device and to logical ones, such as the software that turns a print file into an image. The module is written in SMIv2 and uses the requirement words MUST, SHOULD and MAY in the sense of RFC 2119.

The RFC draws a line around its subject. Managing printing as a whole covers generating the file to be printed, selecting a printer, choosing printing properties, routing, queuing, resource management, scheduling, and finally printing and notifying the user. All of that is outside the model here. Only the management of the printer itself is covered.

Information about printers falls into three categories. Descriptions convey the configuration and capabilities of the printer and its parts. This information is largely static, changing only when the printer is repaired, reconfigured or upgraded. Status is the current operating state of the printer and its parts, so a manager can tell whether a sub-unit is ready to print or is in a state that prevents printing. Alerts are reportable events, meaning changes in the state of the printer that matter to a management application, typically because they affect the printer's ability to print.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC gives a standard list of values about a printer, so that any monitoring tool can ask the same questions and get the same answers. It covers the printer itself, not the whole job of printing a document. The values fall into three groups: what the printer is, what it is doing now, and what has just gone wrong.

sections.title: The Printer Model
sections.content:
The model has three parts. First, print data travels in over a physical connection running some form of transport protocol stack. The data appears on a channel, which is the input to an interpreter. The interpreter converts the print data into a form suitable for marking on the media.

Second, media resides in input sub-units, where it is selected, and is then transported via a media path first to a marker, which produces the marks, and then onto an output sub-unit, with optional finishing operations applied. Third, auxiliary sub-units facilitate control of the printer, inquiry and control of the operator panel, reporting of alerts, and adaptation of the printer to various natural languages and character sets.

All the software sub-units run on the system controller, which stands for the processor, memory and storage systems of the printer. The controller can range from a simple single processor system to a multiprocessor system, and the printer is modelled as having one system controller even when it has more than one processor.

The RFC warns that the sub-units of a printer do not necessarily relate directly to any physically identifiable mechanism. A sub-unit can be a set of definable logical processes, such as an interpreter for a page description language or a command processor that sets operating modes. Every sub-unit other than Alerts reports only state information, either a description or a status. The Alerts sub-unit reports event information.
sections.plainLanguage: The model splits a printer into parts that move data and parts that move paper. Print data arrives on a channel, and an interpreter converts it into something that can be marked on the page. Paper starts in an input, passes a marker that marks it, and ends in an output. Some of these parts are software rather than hardware.

sections.title: The Thirteen Sub-Unit Groups
sections.content:
A printer is composed of 13 types of sub-units, called groups, and each gets its own group of objects in the MIB.

  • General printer: exactly one per printer. It carries the overall status, allows the printer to be reset, and describes the covers and interlocks.
  • Inputs: the mechanisms that feed media to be marked on into the printer. There is one input sub-unit for each distinctly selectable input address.
  • Media: an extension of the Input Group that describes the media currently in each input sub-unit, not what the input could hold.
  • Outputs: the mechanisms that receive marked media. They are addressed either as mailboxes or as slots into which multiple copies are collated.
  • Finishers: sub-units that perform operations on the media other than marking, such as stapling, punching, binding, inserting or folding. They are described in the companion Finisher MIB, RFC 3806.
  • Markers: the mechanisms that produce marks on the media, together with their associated supplies. In a xerographic process the marker covers both the marking process and the fusing process, so a single marker can have both a toner supply and a fuser supply.
  • Media paths: the mechanisms that move media through the printer and connect the inputs, outputs, markers and finishers. One path may print on one surface only, and another may turn the media over and feed it a second time.
  • System controller: represented by the Host Resources MIB, RFC 2790.
  • Interfaces: represented by the Interfaces Group of MIB-II, RFC 1213 and RFC 2863.
  • Print job delivery channels: the independent sources of print data. Each channel can be enabled, so that print data flows, or disabled, so that it does not.
  • Interpreters: the page description language interpreters and the control language interpreters.
  • Console: at most one operator console, which can be queried and modified remotely. The rules that map printer state onto the console are not standardized, so the console state cannot be reproduced.
  • Alerts: detects reportable events, makes an entry in the alert table and, if and only if the event is critical, initiates a trap.

The localization part of the general printer sub-unit identifies the natural language, country and character set in which certain strings are expressed. There may be one or more localizations per printer, listed in the Localization table. Localization SHOULD only be performed on strings named xxxDescription or prtConsoleDisplayBufferText. The agent SHALL return all other character strings in coded character sets in which code positions 0 to 127 are US-ASCII, and SHOULD return them in the UTF-8 transform of ISO 10646 (RFC 3629) to conform to the IETF policy on character sets and languages (RFC 2277). Control codes, at code positions 0 to 31 and 127, SHALL NOT be used unless specifically required in the description of an object.
sections.plainLanguage: The printer is split into thirteen kinds of part, such as paper trays, the marking unit and the operator screen. Each kind has its own table of values that a monitoring tool can read. Some strings, such as descriptions, can be given in the language the printer is set to.

sections.title: Reporting Status at Three Levels
sections.content:
Summary information about the state of the printer is reported at three separate levels. The printer as a whole is reported in the Host Resources MIB. Each sub-unit reports in the principal table of the group that represents it. Alert codes are reported in the Alert Table.

The Host Resources MIB offers three objects that describe a printer: hrDeviceStatus in the device table, hrPrinterStatus in the printer table, and hrPrinterDetectedErrorState in the printer table. The RFC maps its named states onto them. Idle is running(2) and idle(3). Busy or Active is running(2) and printing(4). Non Critical Alert Active is warning(3). Critical Alert Active, Unavailable and Off-line are down(5) and other(1). Moving on-line is down(5) and warmup(5). Standby is running(2) and other(1).

The mapping loses information, and the RFC says so. When both a critical and a non-critical alert are pending, Critical Alert Active prevails, so a manager cannot see that both exist. A printer in Standby is reported as running(2) and other(1), a pair of values that do not uniquely identify that state. The named states the RFC defines are Non Critical Alert Active, Critical Alert Active, Unavailable, Moving on-line or off-line, Standby, Available, Idle, Active and Busy. They are only a subset of the states a printer can be in.

The error state object is an OCTET STRING of 0 to 128 bytes that carries one bit per condition: lowPaper is bit 0, noPaper is bit 1, lowToner is bit 2, noToner is bit 3, doorOpen is bit 4, jammed is bit 5, offline is bit 6, serviceRequested is bit 7, inputTrayMissing is bit 8, outputTrayMissing is bit 9, markerSupplyMissing is bit 10, outputNearFull is bit 11, outputFull is bit 12, inputTrayEmpty is bit 13 and overduePreventMaint is bit 14. Bit 15 is not assigned.

Sub-unit status is reported in the entries of the principal table of the group that represents the sub-unit. For sub-units that report a status, the value is always an integer formed as the sum of five distinct values: Availability, Non-Critical, Critical, On-Line and Transitioning. Availability contributes one of seven values. Available and Idle is 0, Available and Standby is 2, Available and Active is 4, Available and Busy is 6, Unavailable and OnRequest is 1, Unavailable because Broken is 3, and Unknown is 5. Non-critical alerts add 8, critical alerts add 16, an off-line state adds 32, and a sub-unit moving to its intended state adds 64. The syntax range for the whole value is 0 to 126. The RFC's example is an input tray that jammed on the next to last page, which may show a status of 27: unavailable because broken (3), plus a critical state (16) for the jam, plus a non-critical state (8) for low paper.
sections.plainLanguage: Status is reported at three levels: the printer as a whole, each part of the printer, and the list of active alerts. Each part reports its condition as one number built by adding up smaller numbers. The printer's own example is a jammed tray reported as 27. Some detail is lost, because a serious and a minor problem at once show only as the serious one.

sections.title: The Alert Table
sections.content:
The Alert Group consists of a single table in which all active alerts are represented. Each entry holds the severity of the alert, the group and entry where the state change caused the alert, additional information about the alert, and the level of training needed to service it. That additional information is a more detailed location within the sub-unit, an alert code, and a description.

One table is used because a single entry in a group can cause more than one alert. A media path can jam in more than one place at once. Associating the extra information with the entry in the affected group would allow only one report, while associating it with the alert makes multiple reports possible. Every time an alert occurs in the printer, the printer makes one or more entries into the alert table.

The printer decides whether an event is critical or non-critical. A critical alert is triggered by entry into a state in which the printer is stopped and printing cannot continue until the condition is eliminated, such as out of paper, toner empty or output bin full. A non-critical alert is triggered by an event that enters a state in which printing is not stopped, such as input media low, toner low or output bin nearly full, or one that simply reports information, such as a configuration change. The severity object has the values other(1), critical(3), warning(4) and warningBinaryChangeEvent(5).

When the severity is critical, the printer sends a trap or event notification to the host indicating that the table has changed. Whether or not a trap is sent, the RFC expects the management application to poll the printer on a regular basis and to read and parse the table, because polling is what makes the information reliable.

The alert index is an incrementing integer initialized to 1 when the printer is reset, so the first event placed in the table after a reset has the index value 1. Each new alert takes the next higher value, and if the index reaches its maximum the next value used is 1 again. The management application compares the last index it saw with the highest current index to learn that entries were added or removed. The prtAlertTime object gives the value of sysUpTime when the alert was generated, and the training level says whether the alert needs no intervention at all, an untrained person, a trained person, a field service person, or a manager.
sections.plainLanguage: The printer keeps one table of the problems it has right now. Each row says how serious the problem is, which part of the printer caused it, what kind of problem it is, and how hard it is to fix. A serious problem also sends a notification, but the tool is expected to read the table regularly as well, because the notification alone is not enough.

sections.title: Binary and Unary Events, and a Full Table
sections.content:
There are basically two kinds of events that produce alerts. A binary change event comes in pairs. The leading edge event enters a state from which there is only one exit, for example going from running to stopped with a paper jam, and the trailing edge event exits that state, for example fixing the paper jam. Only the leading edge event makes an entry in the alert table. That entry persists until the trailing edge event occurs, which is signalled by the removal of the leading edge entry. A trailing edge event does not create an entry of its own.

A unary change event is not a binary change. The state of the machine has changed, but to a state that is often just as valid as the state that was left, and from which no return is necessary. The RFC's example is an operator changing the paper in the primary input source from letter to legal. The paper may later be changed back to letter, or it may be changed to executive instead. It is therefore not obvious how long to keep unary change event entries in the table. If they were never removed, the table would grow indefinitely.

The agent needs an algorithm for a table that is full and needs new entries. The RFC gives the order to choose an old alert to delete. First, find a non-critical unary alert and delete it, and if there are several, the oldest is suggested. If there are no non-critical unary alerts, find a non-critical binary alert and delete it, again the oldest first. Only then, as a last resort, find a critical binary alert and delete it, oldest first. All critical alerts are binary. Implementers are encouraged to provide at least enough storage space for the maximum number of critical alerts that could occur simultaneously.

If a critical binary alert has been deleted from the table, and space allows and the alert condition still exists, the alert should be re-added even if there was no subsequent transition into the associated state. The RFC recommends the same for non-critical binary alerts. The new entry does not have the same index as the original. Because the alert index is a monotonically increasing integer, there are gaps in the table when an alert is deleted, and the management application may want to re-acquire the printer state and check for changes it did not observe.
sections.plainLanguage: Some problems come in pairs, such as a jam that starts and is later cleared, so the printer removes the entry when the problem is fixed. Other events have no ending, such as changing the paper size, and the printer has to decide when to drop them. When the list is full, the printer drops the least serious entries first, and the oldest of those.

sections.title: Writable Objects and Required MIB Groups
sections.content:
Some objects reflect the existence or amount of a resource inside the printer, such as the size and number of sheets in a paper tray, and most printers lack sensors for every property of every resource. A management application is allowed to write into objects that hold descriptive or existence values for printers that cannot sense these values. Two conditions apply. The printer must behave differently if the installation is reported than if it is not, so the object is not a place to put information the printer does not use, and the printer believes what it is told and acts as if the information were true. On a printer that cannot sense the size, if one paper size is loaded but another size is set into the paper size object, the printer uses the size that was set in its imaging and paper handling. The RFC calls this out by saying the object is not to be used as a sticky note.

Whether the value of a read-write object may actually be changed depends on the implementation, and the RFC notes that any read-write object may behave this way. It is an implementation-specific matter whether MIB object values persist across power cycles or cold starts, with one exception. It is particularly important that prtMarkerLifeCount persist throughout the lifetime of the printer, so if the value of any MIB object persists across power cycles, then prtMarkerLifeCount must also persist.

A Printer MIB implementation also has to support groups from other MIB specifications. All objects in the system group of MIB-II, RFC 1213, shall be implemented. The storage and device groups of the Host Resources MIB, RFC 2790, shall be implemented to support the printer's system controller and any supporting devices, while other Host Resources groups may be implemented if the implementer judges it appropriate. All objects in the Interfaces Group of MIB-II shall be implemented for all print information interfaces to the printer, including non-network interfaces.

The conformance statements at the end of the Printer MIB module list the mandatory groups of the module itself: the general, input, output, marker, media path, channel, interpreter, console and alert table groups. The object groups added for version 2 are optional and appear in GROUP clauses rather than MANDATORY-GROUP clauses. Every object with a MAX-ACCESS of read-write also has a MIN-ACCESS of read-only, so an implementer may expose a writable object as read-only.
sections.plainLanguage: Some values describe things the printer cannot work out for itself, such as the size of the paper in a tray. A tool may write them, and the printer then trusts them and acts on them. A printer that follows this RFC must also report the basic system information, its storage and devices, and its interfaces, because other MIBs define those. Most of the printer's own tables are required, but the tables added in version 2 are optional, and any writable value may be offered as read-only instead.

sections.title: Enumerations and the IANA Printer MIB
sections.content:
Enumerations are sets of symbolic values defined for use with one or more objects. Instead of repeating the list in the syntax clause of each individual object, a commonly used set is given a symbolic data type name, called a textual convention. The Printer MIB and the companion IANA Printer MIB define one category of textual convention each, according to the process that controls the addition of new enumerations.

A Type 1 convention has all of its legal values defined in the Printer MIB, so an additional enumerated value requires the publication of a new Printer MIB. A Type 2 convention has all of its legal values registered in the IANA Printer MIB, so an additional value requires a Designated Expert Review as defined in RFC 2434. The Designated Expert is selected by the IETF Area Director or Directors of the Applications Area. A textual convention is defined in one of these two ways when it is used more than once in the Printer MIB itself, imported and used in the companion Finisher MIB, or imported and used in any other MIB module, including vendor private ones.

The IANA Printer MIB is published in section 5 of the RFC and holds the shared conventions, among them PrtCoverStatusTC, PrtChannelTypeTC, PrtAlertGroupTC, PrtAlertTrainingLevelTC and PrtAlertCodeTC. Its object identifier is mib-2 109. The Printer MIB module itself has the object identifier mib-2 43. The RFC says the initial version of the IANA Printer MIB is to be archived by IANA and subsequently maintained according to the process in section 2.4.1, and that the most current and authoritative version is the one IANA publishes.

For objects with the syntax Integer32, the MIB defines three special values for conditions outside the normal numeric range: other(-1), unknown(-2) and partial(-3). The partial value means that some supply or capacity remains but the amount is indeterminate. The Integer32 range field of an object indicates in which objects these special values are valid.
sections.plainLanguage: Some values in the MIB come as a named list, such as the list of possible alert codes. Each list has a rule for who may add a new entry to it. Some lists can only change with a new version of this RFC. Others live in a separate list that IANA keeps, where a named expert reviews requests to add a value.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 1759
sections.content:
RFC 3805 supersedes and replaces RFC 1759. A compliant implementation of RFC 1759 is also compliant with this document, because the nine new objects are optional, so the update is backward compatible.

The list of changes is long. New objects cover the printer name and serial number, the startup and banner sheets in a new Auxiliary Sheet Group, an Input Switching Group, and counters of critical alert events and of all alert events. Most enumerations became textual conventions, and 28 textual conventions were added. The alert codes were updated to include generic codes, and an optional unary change event alertRemovalOfBinaryChangeEntry(1801) was added. The error state bit coverOpen was renamed doorOpen to match RFC 2790, and the alert codes doorOpen(501) and doorClosed(502) were deprecated in favour of coverOpened(3) and coverClosed(4). All objects with a MAX-ACCESS of read-write now also have a MIN-ACCESS of read-only.

Five new object groups were created, holding the nine new objects, and one new notification group holds the printerV2Alert trap. The RFC also split its references into normative and informative groups, added top level sections for IANA and internationalization considerations, added ranges to all objects with a syntax of Integer32, and removed the CodedCharSet textual convention in favour of an import of IANACharset.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the printer question list. A printer that answers the first edition's questions still passes, because the new questions and the new tables are optional. The main additions cover the printer's name and serial number, startup and banner pages, and counters of how many alerts have happened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are a number of management objects defined in this MIB module with a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create. Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The RFC lists each of them with the harm that misuse could cause, from possible data loss for prtGeneralReset to possible severe inconvenience for prtConsoleDisable, prtGeneralPrinterName and prtGeneralSerialNumber.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, there is then no control over who on that network is allowed to access and GET or SET the objects in this MIB module. The RFC RECOMMENDS that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy. Deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is then the responsibility of the operator to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB module is configured so that access is given only to those principals that have legitimate rights to GET or SET the objects.

Where the operational capability of the printing device is especially vulnerable or difficult to administer, certain objects have been tagged READ-ONLY, preventing modification. For all read-write objects, the conformance guidelines state that vendors are free to implement these objects as READ-ONLY, which covers cases where specific vendor vulnerabilities differ from product to product.
sections.plainLanguage: Some values in the printer can be changed over the network, and changing the wrong one can stop printing or lose work. The RFC says to use the third version of SNMP, which has authentication and privacy, and to configure it so that only the right people can read or change these values.

viz.caption: THE THREE KINDS OF PRINTER INFORMATION

items.title: Descriptions
items.text: Configuration and capabilities. Largely static, changing when the printer is repaired, reconfigured or upgraded.

items.title: Status
items.text: The current operating state of the printer and its various sub-units.

items.title: Alerts
items.text: Reportable events, meaning changes of state that matter to a management application.
